danish.title: Sjette bog (1808–10) — Kapitel 22
paragraphs: Næste dag, efter at være inviteret af greven, spiste fyrst Andrej middag hos familien Rostov og tilbragte resten af dagen der.

Alle i huset forstod, for hvis skyld fyrst Andrej kom, og uden at skjule det forsøgte han at være sammen med Natásha hele dagen. Ikke blot i den forskræmte, men lykkelige og henrykte Natáshas sjæl, men i hele huset herskede der en følelse af ærefrygt for noget vigtigt, der måtte ske. Grevinden så med triste og strengt alvorlige øjne på fyrst Andrej, når han talte med Natásha, og begyndte sky en eller anden kunstig samtale om ligegyldige ting, så snart han så hendes vej. Sonja var bange for at forlade Natásha og bange for at være i vejen, når hun var sammen med dem. Natásha blev bleg af forventningens panik, når hun et øjeblik var alene med ham. Fyrst Andrej overraskede hende med sin forlegenhed. Hun følte, at han ville sige hende noget, men ikke kunne tage sig sammen til det.
Om aftenen, da fyrst Andrej var taget af sted, gik grevinden hen til Natásha og hviskede: »Nå, hvad?«
»Mama! Spørg mig for Guds skyld ikke om noget nu! Man kan ikke tale om det,« sagde Natásha.

Men alligevel lå Natásha den nat længe i sin moders seng, snart ophidset, snart bange, og stirrede lige frem for sig. Hun fortalte, hvordan han havde komplimenteret hende, hvordan han fortalte, at han skulle rejse til udlandet, spurgte hende, hvor de ville tilbringe sommeren, og derefter hvordan han havde spurgt om Boris.

»Men sådan en... sådan en... er aldrig sket for mig før!« sagde hun. »Bare jeg er bange i hans nærhed. Jeg er altid bange, når jeg er sammen med ham. Hvad betyder det? Betyder det, at det er det ægte? Ja? Mama, sover du?«
»Nej, min skat. Jeg er selv bange,« svarede moderen. »Gå nu og sov!«

»Alligevel kan jeg ikke sove. Hvilket vrøvl, at sove! Mor! Mor! Sådan noget er aldrig sket for mig!« sagde hun, overrasket og skræmt over den følelse, hun mærkede i sig selv. »Og kunne vi nogen sinde have tænkt!...«

Natásha syntes, at allerede den gang, hun første gang så fyrst Andrej i Otrádnoe, var hun blevet forelsket i ham. Det var, som om hun frygtede denne mærkelige, uventede lykke ved at møde netop den mand, hun dengang havde valgt (hun var fuldt overbevist om, at hun havde gjort det), og at opdage, at han tilsyneladende ikke var ligegyldig over for hende.

»Og det måtte ske, at han kom netop til Petersborg, mens vi er her. Og det måtte ske, at vi mødtes ved det bal. Det er skæbnen. Det er tydeligt, at det er skæbnen, at alt førte hen til dette! Allerede dengang, straks jeg så ham, følte jeg noget særligt.«
»Hvad sagde han ellers til dig? Hvad er det for vers? Læs dem...« sagde moderen eftertænksomt og hentydede til nogle vers, fyrst Andrej havde skrevet i Natáshas stambog.
»Mama, behøver man ikke at skamme sig over, at han er enkemand?«
»Nej, Natásha! Bed til Gud. 'Ægteskaber sluttes i Himlen,'« sagde moderen.
»Kære, elskede mor, hvor jeg elsker dig! Hvor er jeg lykkelig!« råbte Natásha, fældede tårer af glæde og begejstring og omfavnede sin mor.
Netop på det tidspunkt sad fyrst Andrej hos Pierre og fortalte ham om sin kærlighed til Natásha og sit faste forsæt om at gøre hende til sin hustru.

Den dag havde grevinde Hélène (Pierres hustru) selskab i sit hjem. Den franske ambassadør var der, og en udenlandsk prins af blodet, som i den seneste tid hyppigt besøgte hende, og mange glimrende damer og herrer. Pierre, der var kommet ned fra oven, gik gennem stuerne og slog alle med sit optagne, adspredte og triste udtryk.

Siden ballet havde han følt et anfald af nervøs nedtrykthed nærme sig og havde gjort desperate anstrengelser for at bekæmpe den. Siden hans kones fortrolighed med den kongelige prins var Pierre uventet blevet gjort til kammerherre, og fra da af havde han begyndt at føle sig trykket og skamfuld i hoffets selskab, og mørke tanker om alt menneskeliges forgængelighed kom til ham oftere end før. Samtidig understregede den følelse, han havde bemærket mellem sin protegé Natásha og fyrst Andrej, hans tungsind ved kontrasten mellem hans egen stilling og hans vens. Han forsøgte ligeligt at undgå at tænke på sin kone og på Natásha og fyrst Andrej; og igen syntes alt ham ubetydeligt sammenlignet med evigheden; igen meldte spørgsmålet sig: hvad nytter det? Og han tvang sig til at arbejde dag og nat med frimureropgaver i håb om at fordrive den onde ånd, der truede ham. Hen mod midnat, efter at have forladt grevindens gemakker, sad han ovenpå i en lurvet slobrok og kopierede den skotske frimurerloge-protokol ved et bord i sit lave, tobaksrøgsfyldte værelse, da nogen trådte ind. Det var fyrst Andrej.

»Nå, er det dig!« sagde Pierre med et optaget, utilfreds udtryk. »Og jeg, ser du, er i fuld gang.« Han pegede på sit manuskript med den mine af flugt fra livets ulykker, som ulykkelige mennesker betragter deres arbejde med.
Fyrst Andrej, med et strålende, ekstatisk udtryk af fornyet liv i ansigtet, standsede foran Pierre, og uden at lægge mærke til hans triste blik smilede han til ham med glædens egoisme.
»Nå, kære ven,« sagde han, »jeg ville fortælle dig det i går, og i dag er jeg kommet for at gøre det. Jeg har aldrig oplevet noget lignende. Jeg er forelsket, min ven!«
Pludselig sukkede Pierre dybt og dumpede sin tunge krop ned i sofaen ved siden af fyrst Andrej.
»I Natásha Rostova, ikke sandt?« sagde han.

»Ja, ja! Hvem ellers skulle det være? Jeg ville aldrig have troet det, men følelsen er stærkere end jeg. I går pinte og led jeg, men jeg ville ikke bytte selv den pine for noget i verden. Jeg har ikke levet hidtil. Nu lever jeg endelig, men jeg kan ikke leve uden hende! Men kan hun elske mig?... Jeg er for gammel til hende... Hvorfor siger du ikke noget?«

»Jeg? Jeg? Hvad sagde jeg til dig?« sagde Pierre pludselig, idet han rejste sig og begyndte at gå frem og tilbage i værelset. »Det har jeg altid tænkt... Den pige er en skat... hun er en enestående pige... Min kære ven, jeg bønfalder dig, lad være med at filosofere, lad være med at tvivle — gift dig, gift dig, gift dig!... Og jeg er sikker på, at der ikke vil findes en lykkeligere mand end dig.«
»Men hun?«
»Hun elsker dig.«
»Snak ikke vrøvl...« sagde fyrst Andrej smilende og så Pierre i øjnene.
»Det gør hun, det ved jeg,« råbte Pierre lidenskabeligt.
»Men hør nu,« svarede fyrst Andrej og holdt ham i armen. »Ved du, i hvilken tilstand jeg er? Jeg er nødt til at tale med nogen om det.«

»Ja, kom, kom. Jeg er meget glad,« sagde Pierre, og hans ansigt ændredes virkelig, hans pande blev glat, og han lyttede med glæde til fyrst Andrej. Fyrst Andrej virkede — og var virkelig — en helt anden, helt ny mand. Hvor var hans tungsind, hans foragt for livet, hans desillusion? Pierre var den eneste, han havde besluttet at tale åbent med, og til ham fortalte han alt, hvad der var i hans sjæl. Nu lagde han dristigt og let planer for en lang fremtid, sagde han ikke kunne ofre sin egen lykke for sin fars luner, og talte om, hvordan han enten ville få sin far til at samtykke i ægteskabet og elske hende, eller ville klare sig uden hans samtykke. Så undrede han sig over den følelse, der havde grebet ham, som over noget fremmed, uafhængigt af ham selv.

»Jeg ville ikke have troet nogen, der fortalte mig, at jeg var i stand til en sådan kærlighed,« sagde fyrst Andrej. »Det er slet ikke den samme følelse, jeg kendte før. Hele verden er nu for mig delt i to halvdele: den ene halvdel er hende, og dér er al glæde, håb og lys; den anden halvdel er alt, hvor hun ikke er, og dér er alt mørke og tungsind...«
»Mørke og tungsind,« gentog Pierre. »Ja, ja, det forstår jeg.«
»Jeg kan ikke lade være med at elske lyset, det er ikke min skyld. Og jeg er meget lykkelig! Forstår du mig? Jeg ved, du er glad på mine vegne.«
»Ja, ja,« bekræftede Pierre og så på sin ven med et rørt og trist udtryk i øjnene. Jo lysere fyrst Andrejs lod forekom ham, desto mørkere syntes hans eget.

english.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 22
paragraphs: The next day, having been invited by the count, Prince Andrew dined with the Rostovs and spent the rest of the day there.

Everyone in the house sensed for whose sake Prince Andrew kept coming, and without pretending otherwise, he tried to be near Natasha all day. Not only in the soul of the frightened yet happy and enraptured Natasha, but throughout the whole house, there was a feeling of awe — as though something important and inevitable was about to happen. The countess looked at Prince Andrew with sad, solemnly serious eyes when he talked to Natasha, and timidly launched into some artificial small talk whenever he glanced her way. Sonya was afraid to leave Natasha alone with him and equally afraid of being in the way. Natasha went pale with nervous anticipation whenever she found herself alone with him for a moment. His shyness astonished her. She felt that he wanted to say something but couldn't bring himself to do it.
That evening, when Prince Andrew had left, the countess went up to Natasha and whispered: "Well, what?"
"Mama! For heaven's sake, don't ask me anything now! One can't talk about it," said Natasha.

But all the same, that night, now agitated and now frightened, Natasha lay for a long time in her mother's bed, staring straight ahead. She told her how he had complimented her, how he'd mentioned going abroad, how he'd asked where they planned to spend the summer, and then how he'd asked about Boris.

"But such a thing... such a thing has never happened to me before!" she said. "Only I feel afraid when I'm with him. I'm always afraid. What does that mean? Does it mean it's the real thing? Yes? Mama, are you asleep?"
"No, my love; I'm frightened myself," answered her mother. "Now go to sleep!"

"I won't be able to sleep anyway. What silliness — to sleep! Mama! Mama! Nothing like this has ever happened to me before," she said, surprised and alarmed by the feeling she was aware of in herself. "And could we ever have imagined!..."

It seemed to Natasha that even the first time she had seen Prince Andrew at Otradnoe she had fallen in love with him. It was as if she feared this strange, unexpected happiness of meeting again the very man she had chosen then — she was firmly convinced she had — and finding him, it seemed, not indifferent to her.

"And it had to happen that he should come to Petersburg while we were here. And it had to happen that we should meet at that ball. It's fate. Clearly it's fate — everything was leading up to this! From the very first moment I saw him I felt something special."
"What else did he say to you? What are those poems? Read them..." said her mother, thinking it over, referring to some verses Prince Andrew had written in Natasha's album.
"Mama, does it matter that he's a widower?"
"Don't, Natasha! Pray to God. 'Marriages are made in heaven,'" said her mother.
"Darling Mama, how I love you! How happy I am!" cried Natasha, shedding tears of joy and excitement and hugging her mother.
At that very moment Prince Andrew was sitting with Pierre, telling him of his love for Natasha and his firm resolve to make her his wife.

That day Countess Helene had a reception at her house. The French ambassador was there, and a foreign prince of the blood who had recently become a frequent visitor, along with many brilliant ladies and gentlemen. Pierre, who had come downstairs, walked through the rooms and struck everyone by his preoccupied, absent-minded, and gloomy air.

Since the ball he had felt the approach of a spell of nervous depression and had been fighting desperately against it. Since the intimacy between his wife and the royal prince, Pierre had unexpectedly been made a gentleman of the bedchamber, and from that time he had begun to feel oppressed and ashamed in court society, and dark thoughts about the vanity of all things came to him more often than before. At the same time, the connection he had noticed between his protegee Natasha and Prince Andrew intensified his gloom by the contrast between his own situation and his friend's. He tried equally hard not to think about his wife, about Natasha, or about Prince Andrew; and yet everything seemed trivial compared with eternity. Again the question kept presenting itself: Why? What for? And he forced himself to work day and night at Masonic studies, hoping to drive away the dark spirit that threatened him. Toward midnight, after he had left the countess's apartments, he was sitting upstairs in a shabby dressing gown, copying out the original documents of the Scottish lodge of Freemasons at a table in his low, smoke-filled room, when someone came in. It was Prince Andrew.

"Ah, it's you!" said Pierre with a preoccupied, dissatisfied look. "And here I am, you see, hard at work." He pointed to his manuscript book with that air of seeking escape from life's troubles with which unhappy people regard their work.
Prince Andrew, with a beaming, ecstatic expression of renewed life on his face, stopped in front of Pierre and, not noticing his sad expression, smiled at him with the self-absorption of joy.
"Well, my dear friend," he said, "I wanted to tell you yesterday and I've come to do it now. I've never felt anything like this before. I am in love, my friend!"
Suddenly Pierre heaved a deep sigh and sank his heavy body down on the sofa beside Prince Andrew.
"With Natasha Rostova, yes?" he said.

"Yes, yes! Who else? I would never have believed it, but this feeling is stronger than I am. Yesterday I tortured myself, I suffered, but I wouldn't trade even that torment for anything in the world. I have not lived until now. Only now am I truly alive, but I can't live without her... But can she love me? I'm too old for her... Why don't you say something?"

"I? I? What did I tell you?" said Pierre, suddenly jumping up and pacing the room. "I always thought so... That girl is such a treasure... she is a rare girl... My dear friend, I beg you, don't analyze it, don't doubt it — marry, marry, marry!... And I'm sure there won't be a happier man on earth than you."
"But what about her?"
"She loves you."
"Don't talk nonsense..." said Prince Andrew, smiling and looking into Pierre's eyes.
"She does — I know it," Pierre declared fiercely.
"But listen," said Prince Andrew, catching him by the arm. "Do you know what state I'm in? I have to talk to someone about this."

"Well, go on, go on. I'm very glad," said Pierre, and his face really did change — his brow smoothed out and he listened to Prince Andrew with evident pleasure. Prince Andrew seemed, and truly was, a completely different, brand-new man. Where was his world-weariness, his contempt for life, his disillusionment? Pierre was the only person he had decided to confide in openly, and to him he poured out everything that was in his soul. Now he boldly and freely made plans for an expansive future, said he could not sacrifice his own happiness to his father's whims, and spoke of how he would either win his father's consent to the marriage and his love for Natasha, or manage without that consent. He marveled at the feeling that had taken hold of him, as at something strange, separate from and independent of himself.

"I wouldn't have believed anyone who told me I was capable of such love," said Prince Andrew. "It's not at all the same feeling I knew before. The whole world is now divided into two halves for me: one half is her, and there all is joy, hope, light; the other half is everything where she is not, and there all is gloom and darkness..."
"Gloom and darkness," repeated Pierre. "Yes, yes — I understand that."
"I can't help loving the light — it's not my fault. And I am very happy! You understand me? I know you're glad for my sake."
"Yes, yes," Pierre agreed, gazing at his friend with a moved and sorrowful expression. The brighter Prince Andrew's future appeared, the darker his own seemed.
